title: Command-line arguments: argc and argv
learningObjectives: Describe main's argc and argv parameters and explain their roles in a hosted C program.
Explain valid argument indexes and the null pointer sentinel at argv[argc].
Validate argc before accessing an argument and treat argument strings as external input.
Parse numeric arguments with strtol and check digit consumption, trailing text and range errors.
Design usage messages and distinct success and failure exit statuses.
Test missing, extra, malformed, boundary and quoted command-line arguments.

understand.concept: A hosted C program can receive command-line arguments through int main(int argc, char *argv[]). argc counts the argument strings. argv points to an array of pointers to null-terminated strings, and argv[argc] is a null pointer. argv[0] conventionally identifies the program but its exact content is implementation-defined and it may be empty when unavailable.
understand.whyItMatters: Command-line interfaces make programs scriptable. Incorrect argc assumptions can access outside the argument array; unvalidated text can cause conversion errors or unsafe file operations.
understand.analogy: A portable C interface is a contract between source code and the implementation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the exact C standard and implementation guarantees.

explain.narrative: Valid indexes range from zero through argc minus one; check argc before reading a particular index. argv[argc] is a sentinel, not another argument. Do not assume argv[0] is an absolute path. Shell quoting determines how text is split before the program receives it. Treat every argument as untrusted text. atoi cannot reliably distinguish invalid input from zero or report range errors. Prefer strtol: set errno to zero, check whether digits were consumed, reject trailing text according to the interface, check ERANGE and enforce the application's range. Print usage errors to stderr. Use EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE; returning from the initial call to main has normal exit semantics. Freestanding C environments may not provide hosted command-line support.

examples.title: Inspect arguments within bounds
examples.explanation: The loop visits only indexes below argc. argv[argc] is the null pointer sentinel. argv[0]'s exact content depends on the host.

examples.title: Validate a numeric command-line argument
examples.explanation: The program validates the argument count, then checks strtol's end pointer, trailing characters, ERANGE and the application's range.

practise.guidedTask: Run a program with no extra arguments, one argument and too many arguments. Predict argc and valid argv indexes.
practise.independentTask: Create a command-line utility accepting a filename and positive count. Validate argument count, parse with strtol, reject trailing characters and out-of-range values, and print usage to stderr.
hints: Check bounds before accessing array elements.
Validate external text before conversion or use.
Use the matching standard-library interface and type.
Test normal, boundary and invalid-input cases.
Record implementation-specific assumptions instead of guessing.
